en: Few remained who could become a people.
Ebegey and wise Kongoy,
I saw Chargyn from afar,
This was precious through all the ages,
Nothing like it could be found on earth,
Of this accursed swine,
If any Kyrgyz fell into his hands,
There seemed no end to what he did.
This land where our cord was cut and our swaddling washed,
This Ala-Too our forefathers tended,
Its true state upon the earth could no longer be seen,
Life would not be set right,
The people who had lived in freedom,
He would not let the people settle in their summer pastures,
He plundered their sustenance and ruined them,
Our lot in this place would not improve.
For this wretch, half the people would spill their blood,
This land would come under his heel,
The people and land of this Kakan remained behind,
His boastful tongue was backed by brute force,
A man must rise to stand against him.
Can a surrounded man prosper?
O dear people, lofty as a mountain,
What course could we take?
Now the enemy is coming,
What remedy could there be?
We have not the strength to fight,
Take heed of what you have been told,
Lion Kenen, heed your words,
I shall turn away from wrath,
Know it, if you agree to these words,
Like the Kyrgyz amid the teeming multitude,
Know that I am one of your people here,
The torment of anger,
Know that you will depart unharmed if you consent.
Ebegey and Köböy said this,
And, having spoken, drew their words to a close,
Hero Jeljetpes then said this,
Look outside, wolf-eyed one,
My enemies will fall and drink blood,
Is the open field my hero's battleground?
Without blood being spilled in that hour,
Without the great conflict becoming famed,
Will he then set about fighting?
If he bows his head before the warriors,
Will all good fortune not depart?
The spirited thoroughbred racer,
The brave man headed by a khan,
Will he not die and pass away in regret?
Let us strike that bristling swine,
Will the fox not catch him in the end?
If an unconquered people bows its head,
Will it not shrink today from what it sees?
Will it not draw near to witness it?
Will it not say that its heart is with me?
He chose his warriors and launched the attack,
Would he not unleash the valiant Kyrgyz?
Would he not cut down whoever resisted?
Would he not send forth warriors sharp as swords?
If one fell into his hands, would he let him go?
Would he not slaughter those seeking protection?
Would he not consume even their mutton?
No trembling khan remained,
Would he not strip the people bare?
Not merely your livestock, but your head,
Would he not make it an object of cruel sport?
What your treasury had yielded,
Would he not seize it before all the world?
Would he not strike anyone who faced him?
His forefather was Aleke,
After him came the warrior Kancha,
Would he not exact blood-price from the Bulgars?
The Kyrgyz cannot attain your vengeance,
Can the small Kyrgyz people not recover?
“Indeed, father, here it is,” he said,
Would he forget the heroes?
Would he not bring down whoever confronted him?
So he spoke of a feud whose end none could reach,
The black host came once again,
Many binding words poured forth,
He told the tale through to its end.
When the warrior Kenen heard this,
His soul boiled like flame,
At the depraved Chinese swine,
You had been an enemy since ancient times,
How could we remain meek?
Humiliating the lion-hearted leader,
Casting Kongur down upon the black earth,
Putting him into Kozu’s wicked hands,
Letting an enemy rule the people.
Bringing disgrace upon your royal head,
Turning both cheeks pale,
That enemy swine,
Inflicting harm upon these Kyrgyz,
Taking away the blessed host,
Turning the khan’s fate black,
Paralyzing both his arms,
Making him livestock that grazes grass,
Reducing all he does to disgrace,
Before the humiliation of that black fiend,
Hero Kenen summoned his courage,
His fury sharpened,
All his massed strength emerged.
Curling over both his cheeks,
Hair rose thick as felt socks,
Blood ready to spill upon the sword appeared,
Victory to the warrior, victory to the hero,
Kenen’s words proved true.
The courageous young men,
Now speaking of hero Kenen,
All the heroes were stirred,
Hero Jankishi pondered,
Widowed women and young children,
If they do not die, will they not see another day?
The army pressed the battle fiercely,
Saying the brave ones must not draw back,
All the champions grew fierce,
The warriors formed up by their ranks,
All the destroyers crowded together,
The young warrior Jeljetpes,
His heroes were stirred,
Mounting thoroughbreds, they knotted their gear,
Without delay, the countless host rode out.
The earth broke up and became dust,
The golden red banner visible a month away,
Kaskagül was a cherished soul,
Kapchyga had become khan,
The champion Jeljetpes,
He was the one who bore the banner.
The earth broke up and became dust,
The ridge tops vanished in confusion,
Unseen, the dust climbed into the sky,
Black masses surged in their thousands,
They streamed without end across the open land.
Would a hero think only of wounded honor?
Would the poor head not suffer humiliation?
Overwhelmed by the furious foe,
The great host truly rode out,
To speak of the forefathers,
Until he finished what he had to say,
Before they could say this or that,
Chongteñir had arrived.
From the swine beneath whom the earth bent,
He truly had an army fit to survive,
He bore a challenge no horse could carry,
He had foes whom he held cheap,
In broad daylight the great host,
Moved onward whole and unharmed,
Along that road by which they came,
The earth swarmed before his frozen gaze,
The Chinese fixed their eyes upon that host,
It made the mountain tops disappear,
Its gaze pierced the peaceful people,
With that custom, alas for those eyes,
A dark, massed host of Chinese,
Such a furious and numerous host,
Saying an opposing cloud had gathered,
When fleeing before the great army,
The people ridden down by China stood alone,
What befell the Kyrgyz was known to God,
They were driven back in confusion,
Chongteñir poured out his venom,
His great frame towered above the rest,
Chongteñir poured out his wrath.
Against the sons of the Kyrgyz stronghold,
Chongteñir wrought calamity,
The Manchu and Shibe thundered,
Together with the Kanday and Solon,
And the black Kalmyks who stood there.
To the Mongols and the Manchus,
To all the great peoples,
Chongteñir issued an order.
Let us dwell upon the extent of his command,
Chongteñir acted thus,
What had been laid out was completed,
You march on, Chongteñir,
Calling it a bitter word against the Kyrgyz,
You lead the people, Chongteñir.
From the edge where the sun rises,
Chongteñir covered them with arrows,
From the north and from the south,
Chongteñir surrounded them with warriors.
Against the Chinese, the Kyrgyz were few,
The multitudes struggled, alas for those brave heads,
Before the Chinese, the people stood alone,
A grievous assault came upon them.
From every side he rained arrows,
The solitary people were hemmed in,
At that time Chongteñir,
Speaking firmly, clad them in armor,
His kingship became known,
Of that raging swine,
His giant prevailed and his challenge prevailed,
Entrusting survival to Almighty God,
Then turning upon the solitary one,
He was indeed that raging master.
Then there came a deep rumble,
Chinese and Chyban—the Kyrgyz were few,
Amid the shattered host,
Leaving neither whip nor storm behind,
They struck broadside in the struggle,
Send the champions into the attack,
All of you, halt and stand fast,
Warriors, form yourselves in ranks.
Then let this be proclaimed,
Arrange it in this manner.
If he is a warrior, if he is a lion,
If he is the bravest of the champions,
Let him come out in single combat, Kyrgyz-style,
Grant him the great turn,
Let us see the measure of his strength,
And what power he has against the Kyrgyz.
Having spoken thus, Chongteñir,
Issued a stern command.
The master of speech cried aloud,
And sent the battle toward the other side,
The red Kyrgyz, the great fighter,
They made ready at every drumbeat,
The war drum deafened the ears,
They had it beaten with a thunderous roar.
Ears deafened and heads grew numb,
It bound mind and senses,
Blood sprayed like sparks,
Across the broad battlefield,
At the place of destruction,
Ozu Khan rode out to single combat.
Like a black boar, like a fox,
The battle cry of Khan Joloy,
The champion stood apart from the others,
He mounted a horse and went against the foe,
Who had ever known such a challenge?
Do not ask what Ozu was like,
It was the day the warrior went forth,
What could a solitary lamb do?
It was a day fought for a half-share of blood,
A day when Jadigöy raised a flame,
In this faithless world.
The day the treasure was gathered and stored.
Do not ask about his bloody words,
Dark-fated was the thought I conceived,
The very heart of harsh misfortune,
Of the punishment that struck your soul,
He has a head as large as a cauldron,
He has a khan who sets things in order,
When he attacks, he makes all sway,
When he surrounds them, he gives no respite,
He takes away the approaching host,
A khan remained who knew no settled place,
The lineage of the wild one,
Living while souls fought beside him,
One who drank and was never sated with blood,
One who spared no life in battle,
Who crushed their steel warriors,
Who crushed even the unmatched wise men,
Raised in the desert breathing poison,
Raised on the crag spilling blood,
